title: Brain, spinal cord, nerves and reflexes
blurb: Match each brain region to its job, layer the meninges, read the spinal cord's roots and sequence a reflex arc.
question: After a stroke, a patient understands everything his nurse says but can barely form words, and a second patient who fell backward now walks with an unsteady, uncoordinated gait. Which brain areas were most likely damaged in each patient?

teach.body: Formally, the brain is divided into the cerebrum, the diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus), the cerebellum and the brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata). In plain English: the cerebrum thinks, senses and moves you on purpose; the diencephalon relays and regulates; the cerebellum smooths and balances movement; and the brainstem keeps you alive. The cerebrum is the largest part: two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum, with an outer cortex of gray matter folded into gyri and sulci.

head: Lobe
Main jobs
rows: Voluntary movement (primary motor cortex), planning, judgment, personality; Broca's area (speech production)
Somatosensory cortex: touch, pain, temperature, body position
Hearing (auditory cortex), Wernicke's area (language comprehension), memory
teach.caption: Broca's area produces speech (usually left frontal); Wernicke's area understands language (temporal).

head: Structure
Main jobs
rows: Relays sensory input to the cortex (all senses except smell)
Homeostasis: temperature, hunger, thirst, water balance; controls pituitary and ANS
Relays cerebrum to cerebellum; helps regulate breathing
Vital centers: heart rate, breathing rhythm, blood pressure; cough, sneeze, swallow, vomit
teach.caption: The limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus) handles emotion and memory.
Note the cerebellum tucked under the occipital lobe, and the brainstem running from the pons down to the medulla, which joins the spinal cord.

letters.word: Pia mater: innermost, on the brain

teach.caption: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), made by the choroid plexus in the ventricles, circulates in the ventricles and the subarachnoid space, cushioning and nourishing the CNS.

teach.h: The spinal cord turns the brain inside out
teach.body: The spinal cord runs from the medulla through the foramen magnum to about L1-L2 in adults; below that is the cauda equina. In the cord, gray matter is INSIDE (a butterfly shape) and white matter is OUTSIDE, the reverse of the cerebrum. Each spinal nerve joins the cord by two roots: the dorsal (posterior) root is sensory, with a dorsal root ganglion holding sensory cell bodies; the ventral (anterior) root is motor. Spinal nerves are mixed.

teach.caption: Where the roots join, the spinal nerve carries both: it is mixed.

steps.label:
Integration
center
steps.sub: In the CNS, often an interneuron

teach.caption: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is monosynaptic: no interneuron. Withdrawal reflexes use interneurons. The cord can act before the brain is aware.

teach.h: Scenario: two patients on the neuro unit
teach.body: Danielle, a nursing applicant, shadows on a neuro unit. Mr. Ruiz had a left frontal stroke: he follows every instruction but struggles to form words, so Broca's area (speech production) is damaged while Wernicke's area (comprehension, temporal lobe) is intact. Mrs. Okafor fell backward and now sways and staggers: her cerebellum, which coordinates balance and fine-tunes movement, was injured. Her breathing and heart rate are steady, so her medulla's vital centers are working.

teach.text: Look-alike pairs: HYPOthalamus runs homeostasis and the pituitary, while the thalamus relays sensation. The cerebellum coordinates movement; breathing belongs to the medulla and pons. Broca's = production, Wernicke's = comprehension. Occipital = vision, temporal = hearing. Dorsal root = sensory. Spinal gray matter is inside.

items: Frontal: movement, judgment, Broca's area. Parietal: touch, pain, temperature. Temporal: hearing, Wernicke's area, memory. Occipital: vision.
Thalamus = sensory relay; hypothalamus = homeostasis and pituitary control; cerebellum = coordination and balance; medulla = heart rate, breathing, blood pressure.
Meninges outer to inner: dura, arachnoid, pia (DAP); CSF from the choroid plexus flows in the ventricles and subarachnoid space.
Spinal cord ends about L1-L2; gray matter inside; dorsal root sensory, ventral root motor.
Reflex arc: receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector. 12 pairs of cranial nerves.

summary: You can now match brain regions, lobes and brainstem parts to their functions, order the meninges, and describe how the spinal cord's gray matter, white matter and roots are arranged. You can also sequence a reflex arc and identify key cranial nerves by function.

A.q: Which brain structure contains the vital centers that regulate heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure?
A.why: The medulla oblongata holds the cardiovascular and respiratory vital centers, plus reflexes such as coughing and swallowing.

whyNot.0: The cerebellar hemispheres coordinate balance and movement; they do not run the vital centers.
whyNot.1: The hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary, not the breathing rhythm.
whyNot.3: The midbrain handles visual and auditory reflexes.

A.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum processes vision?
A.why: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, contains the visual cortex.

whyNot.0: The temporal lobe processes hearing and contains Wernicke's area.
whyNot.1: The parietal lobe processes touch, pain, temperature and body position.
whyNot.2: The prefrontal cortex, part of the frontal lobe, handles planning and judgment, not vision.

A.q: Which sequence lists the meninges from outermost to innermost?
A.why: Dura mater is the tough outer layer, arachnoid is in the middle and pia mater lies directly on the brain (DAP).

whyNot.1: This is the order from innermost to outermost, the reverse of what was asked.
whyNot.2: The dura, not the arachnoid, is the outermost layer.
whyNot.3: The arachnoid lies between the dura and the pia; the pia is innermost.

B.q: A tumor in one brain structure disrupts a patient's body temperature, thirst and pituitary hormone output. Which structure is most likely affected?
B.why: The hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance, and it controls the pituitary gland.

whyNot.0: The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex; it does not control the pituitary.
whyNot.2: The pineal gland secretes melatonin for the sleep-wake rhythm.
whyNot.3: The pons relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate breathing.

B.q: What does the dorsal (posterior) root of a spinal nerve contain?
B.why: The dorsal root carries sensory (afferent) fibers into the cord and has the dorsal root ganglion, which holds sensory cell bodies.

whyNot.1: Motor fibers travel in the ventral root, and the ganglion holds sensory cell bodies.
whyNot.2: Motor axons to muscle leave through the ventral (anterior) root.
whyNot.3: The spinal nerve is mixed, but each root is not: the dorsal root is sensory.

B.q: Which sequence shows the correct order of a reflex arc?
options: Receptor, motor neuron, integration center, sensory neuron, effector
Effector, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, receptor
Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector
Receptor, integration center, sensory neuron, motor neuron, effector
B.why: The receptor detects the stimulus, the sensory neuron carries it to the CNS integration center, and the motor neuron carries the response to the effector.

whyNot.0: The sensory and motor neurons are swapped: sensory comes before integration.
whyNot.1: The arc starts at a receptor and ends at an effector, not the other way round.
whyNot.3: The signal must reach the integration center by way of the sensory neuron first.

C.q: After a stroke, Mr. Lee follows spoken instructions correctly but speaks in slow, broken phrases that he struggles to form. Which area is most likely damaged?
C.why: Understanding is intact but producing speech is impaired, which points to Broca's area in the (usually left) frontal lobe.

whyNot.0: Wernicke's area handles comprehension, which Mr. Lee still has.
whyNot.2: Broca's area is in the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe.
whyNot.3: Wernicke's area is in the temporal lobe and governs comprehension, not production.

C.q: A patient cannot turn his right eye outward (laterally), but its other movements and his pupil reflex are normal. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
C.why: The abducens nerve (VI) moves the eye laterally (abducts it).

whyNot.0: The oculomotor nerve controls most eye movements and pupil constriction, which are normal here.
whyNot.1: The optic nerve carries vision, not eye movement.
whyNot.2: The trigeminal nerve carries face sensation and controls chewing.

C.q: Which statement about the adult spinal cord is correct?
options: Its gray matter lies inside, with white matter outside
Its white matter lies inside, with gray matter outside
It extends down to the sacrum within the vertebral canal
Its ventral roots carry sensory fibers into the cord
C.why: In the cord, gray matter forms an inner butterfly shape surrounded by white matter, the reverse of the cerebrum.

whyNot.1: That arrangement (gray outside, white inside) describes the cerebrum, not the cord.
whyNot.2: The adult cord ends at about L1-L2; below it lies the cauda equina.
whyNot.3: Ventral roots are motor; sensory fibers enter through the dorsal roots.

reteach.title: The brain as an airport
reteach.question: Picture a busy airport: who runs the terminal, the control tower, the life-support systems and the incoming mail? Which brain part is each one?

blocks.body: The cerebrum is the terminal where passengers think, plan and choose where to go. The thalamus is the mailroom: almost every incoming message (all senses except smell) is sorted there before reaching the offices upstairs. The hypothalamus is facilities management: heating, water supply, food, and orders to the pituitary. The cerebellum is ground control, keeping every plane balanced and on line. The medulla is the power plant: if it fails, everything stops, because it runs heart rate, breathing and blood pressure.

blocks.text: The mailroom (thalamus) and facilities (hypothalamus) sit side by side, but only facilities controls the pituitary and body temperature.

explain.body: Lobes handle thinking, sensing and moving. The thalamus relays, the hypothalamus regulates, the cerebellum coordinates and the medulla keeps the vital centers running.

test.q: A patient with a head injury has poor coordination, an unsteady gait and trouble with fine movements, but normal breathing. Which structure is most likely injured?
test.why: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture, so damage causes unsteady, uncoordinated movement.

whyNot.0: Medulla damage would threaten breathing and heart rate, which are normal here.
whyNot.2: The occipital lobe processes vision, not coordination.
whyNot.3: The thalamus relays sensory information; it does not fine-tune movement.

explain.body: Dura (outer), arachnoid (middle), pia (inner). CSF is made by the choroid plexus in the ventricles and circulates in the ventricles and subarachnoid space to cushion and nourish the CNS.

test.why: CSF is made by the choroid plexus in the brain's ventricles.

whyNot.0: The dura mater is the tough outer meninx; it protects but does not make CSF.
whyNot.2: CSF flows in the space beneath the arachnoid, but the arachnoid does not make it.

explain.body: Gray matter inside, white matter outside. Dorsal root sensory, ventral root motor. A reflex arc runs receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector; the knee-jerk is monosynaptic.

test.q: Which statement about the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is correct?
options: It relies on interneurons in the spinal cord
It is routed through the cerebellum
It is monosynaptic, with no interneuron
It is a voluntary response of the leg
test.why: The patellar reflex is monosynaptic: the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron in the spinal cord.

whyNot.0: Withdrawal reflexes use interneurons; the knee-jerk does not.
whyNot.1: The spinal cord processes the reflex before the brain is aware of it.

explain.body: Twelve pairs, numbered I to XII. High-yield: I smell, II vision, III most eye movement, V face sensation, VII facial expression, VIII hearing and balance, X vagus (parasympathetic), XII tongue.

test.q: A patient's vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII) is damaged by a tumor. Which functions are most likely affected?
test.why: The vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) has a cochlear branch for hearing and a vestibular branch for balance.

whyNot.0: Facial expression and taste from the front of the tongue are carried by the facial nerve (VII).
whyNot.2: Face sensation and chewing belong to the trigeminal nerve (V).
whyNot.3: Lateral eye movement is controlled by the abducens nerve (VI).
